reconcile.connective: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read Mark's double crowing as fuller detail, noting the other Gospels report only the last crow Mark also records.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the harder reading: Matthew has one crowing, Mark two — distinct traditions, not compatible details of a single night.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: "Contradictions? What Contradictions? Harmonizing the Gospels." (The Bart Ehrman Blog)
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, "Contradictions? What Contradictions? Harmonizing the Gospels" (The Bart Ehrman Blog, September 13, 2023)

excerpts.excerpt_text: As Mark is the only Evangelist who tells us that our Lord predicted that the cock should crow twice (Mar 14:30), so he only mentions that it did crow twice (Mar 14:72). The other Evangelists, who tell us merely that our Lord predicted that "before the cock should crow he would deny Him thrice" (Mat 26:34; Luk 22:34; Joh 13:38), mention only one actual crowing, which was Mark's last.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB directly compares Mark's double cock-crow (predicted and fulfilled) against the other three Gospels' single mention, explaining the count difference as selective detail rather than conflict — squarely on this contradiction's question of when/how often the cock crowed.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the cock-crow count directly under 'Peter's denials at one time / At another time' (pp. 424-425), citing Warington, Alford, and Whitby for the once-vs-twice reconciliation.
